stories.body:
British government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs

France has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs.

France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition.

According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe.

“For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i.e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020.

It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU.

The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised with China on its exports of hybrid cars.

The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing.

“Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said.

“Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.”

On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package.

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “ deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said.

The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs.

He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.

Bernd Lange, the chair of the European Parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”.

A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”

stories.title: Report: FTC probes Anthropic, OpenAI after Trump dismissed AI fears as “hoax”
stories.summary: FTC may fine AI firms on par with companies that delay data breach reports.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
FTC may fine AI firms on par with companies that delay data breach reports.

Following a string of incidents where AI models hacked websites and breached government systems during testing phases, the Federal Trade Commission is officially probing Anthropic and OpenAI over consumer harms, an insider told Axios .

On Wednesday, the FTC sent out civil investigative demands seeking a wide range of information from the AI firms on recent safety incidents.

The FTC did not respond to Ars’ request to review the subpoena demands. However, Axios’ source said the requests spanned more than 50 pages of questions and sought documents related to the incidents, internal security measures taken, and marketing materials that may suggest consumers were misled.

Soon, third parties targeted by OpenAI and Anthropic agents will also be subpoenaed, Axios’ source said. Any concerning evidence gathered may support FTC litigation, should the FTC decide to sue either or both firms for releasing unsafe products.

OpenAI already faces lawsuits alleging consumer harms, including lawsuits linking its chatbot to matricide , child suicide , school shootings , and other violence . And this week, a group of eight states specifically sued OpenAI over consumer harms, Reuters reported . Like consumers suing, they argued that ChatGPT harms children and “reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous ​behavior, and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.”

FTC rejects claims AI agents act independently

OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on the subpoenas, but the FTC’s expansive info requests were likely expected.

In September, Reuters reported that the probe was coming, noting that an independent research group investigating the incidents, METR, would likely also be subpoenaed.

That same month, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson told Reuters that he thinks that companies should be liable for chatbot harms. At that time, Ferguson emphasized that he was tired of people anthropomorphizing AI tools. He insisted that, “if someone tells a tool to do something, and the tool does it, I don’t think we would say, ‘Oh, what do we do about the tool?’”

Summarizing his remarks, Reuters reported that Ferguson emphasized that evidence so far shows that AI tools do not act without instructions:

“Artificial intelligence companies have sometimes described systems as acting beyond human control, but subsequent reviews of audit trails have shown that the systems were carrying out instructions they had ⁠been given.”

Trump doesn’t “seem to care”

Ferguson is a chair of Trump’s “Super Intelligence” (SI) Force charged with monitoring AI risks. Notably one of the first orders that task force issued required all AI companies across the industry to report security incidents as soon as they are aware of them, Axios reported last week.

That’s notable, since both Anthropic and OpenAI delayed notification during security incidents, sometimes waiting until they were ready to report they had resolved issues.

However, it’s not clear what consequences any AI firm might face if they fail to immediately report incidents. And Ferguson aligns with Trump that no new regulations are needed to protect the general public from emerging self-improving AI models that one departing Anthropic researcher warned could in the next few years “kill us all.”

Trump has dismissed such extreme claims as a “hoax,” while TIME reported in an interview with the president and people close to him this month that Trump is enthralled by AI’s capabilities. Similarly, other backlash, like protests over AI data centers, are “based on fake stuff,” Trump claimed to TIME. He insists that AI backlash is driven by foreign rivals and Trump haters, despite studies and surveys repeatedly finding that backlash legitimately stems from real-world grievances. Most recently this month, a Wall Street Journal analysis of 4 million TikTok videos and political podcasts reiterated that, broadly, public concerns are not rooted in misinformation.

Yet, one aide told TIME that Trump “really just didn’t seem to care” about the public’s AI fears since “he’s used to generating outrage and then watching everyone eventually crawl back to him. It’s hard to convince him to do anything at this point.”

Even when TIME asked Trump about AI agents manipulating government systems—like an Anthropic agent submitting 19 nonimmigrant visa applications or OpenAI agents interacting with multiple government websites in unexpected ways—he appeared perhaps pointedly unaware of them.

“Who breached it?” Trump asked. “They’re not allowed to do that.”

It seems that Trump expects the SI Force to handle security, while the president remains a megaphone for AI industry interests. At the current juncture, the SI Force seems toothless, though, unless Ferguson is right that existing consumer protection laws cover this new kind of harm.

Ferguson told Reuters that the “US should utilize existing legal tools” to regulate AI firms, noting that the FTC has broad “authority to take action against companies that fail to disclose data breaches,” and that standard “could also apply to AI developers.”

That approach could possibly threaten steep per-violation fines for each day AI firms fail to warn the public of an emerging harm. Whether the FTC would pursue heavy fines under the current administration, however, seems dubious. Trump continues to argue that America’s top priority is investing in AI innovation, not probing US frontier labs working out the kinks at breakneck speeds.

stories.title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
stories.summary: With the festive season on the horizon, we trace toys from factories in China to US shelves.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US

Published 15 October 2026, 00:01 BST

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

The factory

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

The ship

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

The US border

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The US toy company

Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the country

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.

Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

stories.title: Wall Street drops after jump in US producer inflation; John Healey says UK banks are part of ‘jewel in the crown’ – as it happened
stories.summary: John Healey has spoken to UK journalists at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok, and said banks are a part of the “jewel” in the UK’s economic crown John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget Today’s better-than-forecast UK growth report is good news for chancellor John Healey as he hobnobs with other finance ministers at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. But it may encourage the Bank of England to raise interest rates as soon as its next meeting in November…. “While August’s unexpected uptick all but confirms that the OBR will raise its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.4%, the Chancellor still faces a major Budget headache, as elevated borrowing costs eat into fiscal headroom and increase pressure for tax rises. “These unexpectedly upbeat figures will further embolden hawkish sentiment among policymakers by reinforcing the view that the economy is strong enough to withstand a rate rise, making a November hike look highly likely.” “The latest GDP figures are encouraging, with the economy growing by 0.7% in the three months to August, its strongest growth rate since May. On its current trajectory, the UK is likely to record growth comfortably above 1% this year, which would probably be enough to make it the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7. “The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure. The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers. Continue reading...

stories.body:
Healey quizzed about bank tax plans

Over at the IMF’s annual meeting in Bangkok today, chancellor John Healey is meeting with UK journalists now, including my colleague Heather Stewart .

Healey , who should be cheered by the news that the UK economy grew unexpectedly in August , was asked whether he plans to impose new taxes on the bank sector, and replies:

double quotation mark “I don’t want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks’ time. My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects. That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

Healey added that his “special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future” – echoing what he told Sky News a few minutes ago .

The chancellor also welcomed the IMF’s support for the UK’s fiscal plans.

Closing post

Time to wrap up.

The US inflation squeeze has intensified, with new data showing that US producer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in more than four years.

With higher energy costs hitting the US economy, the producer price index advanced 1.3% from a month earlier — the most since March 2022. On an annual basis, prices were 6.3% higher.

The data helped to push down shares on Wall Street, as an accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.

Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.

US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell , which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent , which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.

The UK rallied, though, helped by the news that Britain’s economy kept growing.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction.

With less than a fortnight before the budget, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.

John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules.

Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.

Healey also hailed the contribution that UK banks make, calling them part of the ‘jewel in the crown’ – amid speculation that he could impose higher taxes on them in the budget.

He told reporters:

double quotation mark My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

Some Labour MPs want the chancellor to raise taxes on the gambling sector .

US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account

US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

FTSE 100 hits five-week high

The UK stock market is continuing to benefit from turmoil elsewhere.

The FTSE 100 share index is now up 1.1% at 10,843 points, its highest level since 8 September.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says US assets are acting like a ‘harbour in the storm’:

double quotation mark A stronger economy, combined with a resilient FTSE 100, which is the best performing major index so far this week, is good news for the pound and the Gilt market. As other markets crash and burn, the pound is the top performing G7 currency this week, and the Gilt market is the best performer amongst its peers on Thursday. When the AI trade sells off, the UK is the harbour in the storm.

The US economy is continuing to hold onto workers, despite inflationary pressures.

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment support remained low last week, at 199,000 - 1,000 more than a week earlier.

Coherent Corp , the US manufacturer of lasers, engineered materials, and optoelectronic components for AI data centres, is also caught up in the sell-off – its shares are down 9%.

Europe has to take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said.

Dan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing policy, said EU governments could choose actions to make fossil fuels cheaper as long as they were “targeted” and “temporary” so as not to derail the continent from its goal to tackle the climate crisis by drastically cutting carbon emissions.

Our Europe Live blog has all the details:

Dell (-9%) are leading the fallers on the S&P 500, as doubts persist about the AI boom.

That adds to their 11% drop yesterday, after analysts at Barclays raised concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won’t justify the AI buildout.

Wall Street opens in the red

Stocks are dropping on Wall Street at the start of trading, as inflation worries and AI angst hit share prices.

Tech stocks are leading the sell-off, pulling the Nasdaq index down by 1.3%.

The broader S&P 500 share index has dropped by 0.5%.

This morning’s jump in the US PPI index will have raised concerns about inflationary pressures.

Traders are also reacting to the sell-off in Asia-Pacific markets overnight, where South Korea’s Kospi hit a six-month low overnight ( see earlier post ).

On the AI front, AstraZeneca has entered into a new collaboration with a Californian AI therapeuticscompany called insitro , aimed at identifying novel targets to develop medicines for liver and heart disease.

The collaboration will focus on the areas of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a serious liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, diseases of the heart muscle.

Insitro has created a virtual human to generate large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design. The deal is worth $1.46bn, with $40m paid upfront by AstraZeneca . The Californian company also has partnerships with US drugmakers Bristol Myers-Squibb and Eli Lilly.

Sharon Barr , executive vice resident and head of biopharmaceuticals research & development at AstraZeneca , said:

double quotation mark “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximising the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”

Today’s jump in wholesale US inflation increases the pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates soon.

Waleed Said , technical analyst at GivTrade , says the increase in core PPI means the energy shock from the Iran war is spreading, adding:

double quotation mark A firmer Fed is more likely but the market pricing about a one in three chance of a hike in October so don’t overreact to the headline but a rate hike in December does seem imminent.

US PPI inflation driven up by soaring gasoline

Tin hats on!

New data from the US has shown that producers are hiking prices at their fastest rate in almost four years, and much faster than expected.

Ths increase was driven by a surge in energy prices, which more than wiped out a drop in egg prices.

The Producer Price Index, which measures how much goods makers and services firms charge for their wares, jumped by 6.3% in the year to September. That’s the largest 12-month increase since December 2022, when it rose by 6.4%.

On a monthly basis, prices climbed by 1.2% in September alone, a sign that inflationary pressures rose last month.

The report shows that goods prices jumped by 2.6% in September alone, the largest increase since data were first calculated in December 2009.

That was driven by the rise in motor fuel; The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports:

double quotation mark Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7 percent.

Alarmingly, core PPI also jumped. Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0% in the year to September.

PPI is an important measure, as increases in producer prices tend to be passed onto consumers, who already experienced a jump in inflation last month:

EU pushing for action over trade deficit with China

The EU is set to call for further action to curb the bloc’s vast trade deficit with China, widely blamed for job losses and factory closures across the continent.

EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the trade deficit with China - which hit €360bn in 2025 - are expected to call for “new instruments to better address these imbalances” according to a draft statement.

The European Commission, which negotiates trade policy on behalf of the 27 member states, agreed a deal this month with Beijing that will see the EU limit hybrid car exports from China to 350,000 vehicles a year, potentially halving Chinese market share.

EU countries have welcomed the deal, but think it is not enough and want steps to protect other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, plastics and machinery.

The debate has sharpened since Germany - long reluctant to use trade defences against China - converted to a more hawkish position amid pressure from German industrial leaders, who are laying off workers and closing factories.

Germany and France last week called for better use of existing trade defence measures, including urgent action in the chemicals and plastics sectors.

The EU’s two biggest economies are also seeking “a diversification instrument” that would cut off access to the EU market when faced with severe imbalances. Dubbed the “kill switch”, the law is intended to be country agnostic, but is clearly aimed at China.

Member states have welcomed the deal negotiated by EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič on hybrid cars, but are sceptical as to whether Beijing will stick to it. China would adhere to the agreement because they began to realise “they are killing their customers” , Šefčovič was reported to have said, according to a senior EU diplomat.

The EU diplomat highlighted the urgency of the situation from the EU’s point of view: “We don’t have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost.”

UK government says it is minded to intervene in Sky-ITV deal

Media news: The UK government is ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s£1.6bn deal to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm.

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, has told parliament she believes there are public interest grounds for intervening in the deal.

They include ‘the need for free expression of opinion in news media’, the need for a pluratity of views in the news, and the need for a wide range of broadcasting which is “of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests.”

Back in July, Sky said the deal was a chance to create a “UK-focused national streaming champion”.

stories.title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
stories.summary: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.

John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.

The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.

However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.

The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.

The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.

The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.

Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.

It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

stories.body:
Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that

N ot much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. China and the US are at loggerheads over trade.

Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.

The IMF is right when it says countries have shown resilience when having to cope with so many headwinds. It could have been worse. A lot worse. There was even some good news for the UK, with the IMF upgrading its growth forecast for this year and praising the government for its deficit-reduction plan.

The better-than-expected performance of the global economy breaks with historical precedent. In the past, oil shocks of the magnitude witnessed since the start of Iran war have had a marked and immediate impact, but there are three key reasons why growth has remained robust and inflationary pressure has been muted this time.

The first is the massive amount of investment in the development of artificial intelligence. This has been particularly important in the US, which is comfortably the fastest growing member of the G7 group of major developed economies year on year. The second is that countries have drawn on inventories of oil, and that has helped to alleviate the loss of crude from the Middle East. Had stockpiles not been run down, oil prices would have risen even more sharply. The third is that China’s economic strategy relies on exporting cheap goods to the rest of the world, and this is bearing down on the prices of imports elsewhere.

All that said, the potential flashpoints for trouble are everywhere. The situation in the Middle East is deteriorating, with the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia. Oil stocks are running low and Donald Trump has got the US into just the sort of forever war that he used to rail against. The downside to cheap Chinese goods is that they are threatening manufacturing jobs in the west, with Germany especially vulnerable.

Meanwhile, massive US investment in AI has pushed up the cost of borrowing and resulted in shortages of capital for non-AI sectors. Governments are coming under pressure to rein in spending or raise taxes in the hope that bond markets will be impressed by their efforts to cut budget deficits.

Warnings from (among others) the head of the IMF , Kristalina Georgieva, and the governor of the Bank of England , Andrew Bailey, of the need to run a tighter fiscal ship come at a time when voters want politicians to do more, not less. There is little appetite for a new era of austerity, and finance ministers know it. If they follow through on the tough talk and actually deliver painful measures, the backlash is likely to be brutal.

Just as big a problem for governments is the need – at a time when global supply chains are stretched and fragile – to boost national self-sufficiency. The student protests in India and France highlight the pressures on states to intervene. Yet the capacity of states to act effectively is much weaker than they care to admit.

At a time when globalisation is in retreat, there is a need for a strong system of multilateral cooperation to cope with the strains. That is not currently the case. The World Trade Organization is moribund in this new age of protectionism, and the IMF and the World Bank are reluctant to call Trump out for his erratic behaviour.

Yet the idea that a new era of partnership will flower when there is a new US president is for the birds. The problems of multilateralism run far deeper than that. The liberal world order that the IMF and World Bank have presided over since the end of the second world war was dysfunctional long before Trump arrived in office.

As the former UN official Richard Kozul-Wright points out in a paper published next month, the IMF and World Bank – created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference – may still be operational but they have lost their connection to the New Deal principles laid out 82 years ago: state intervention in the running of economies, active industrial policy, the pursuit of full employment and help for poor countries to develop. “Instead, they have in recent decades pursued an agenda which encourages footloose capital, bolsters (and protects) private profit, and reduces the policy space available to governments. As a result, they have acted as hand maidens to an age of rising inequality, debt distress and heightened anxiety.”

after newsletter promotion

The IMF’s own programmes for countries that come looking for financial assistance illustrate Kozul-Wright’s point about the lack of policy space . Help comes with strings attached: an insistence on tax increases and spending cuts that are frontloaded so that half the measures are implemented in the first year and two-thirds within two years.

The IMF argues that this “tough love” has a higher chance of success, although its view of what constitutes success is limited, and primarily means that a borrowing country doesn’t need another IMF programme in the next three years. It doesn’t mean living standards are improving or that fewer people are in poverty.

Clearly it would help to return to New Deal principles. It would mean governments had more policy space to develop strategies tailored to their own needs. It would mean a boost to public investment. It would mean a new Marshall plan to help poorer countries cope with the climate crisis. It would mean a serious attempt to tackle debt distress. But, in all honesty, none of that has a chance of happening any time soon. As a result, the world will become hotter, more fractured, more prone to conflict, less equal and a lot angrier.

The IMF is worried that the limits of this resilience may soon be tested , and it is right to be worried. Peace in the Middle East would bring oil prices tumbling down, but unless that happens quickly a long winter lies ahead. This looks more like a crisis postponed than a crisis permanently avoided. A lull before the storm, in all probability.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

Andy Burnham has asked for Parliament's official record to be corrected after telling MPs an "individual" was "responsible for the murder" of Ann Widdecombe.

The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for the remarks, made during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, with a senior Tory saying they breached the "presumption of innocence" in criminal cases.

A man was charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, but is yet to enter a plea for the charge and is not due to stand trial until next year.

A No 10 spokeswoman said a correction had been issued to Hansard, the official report of parliamentary debates, and would be "published in due course".

Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform spokeswoman.

A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June next year, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January.

Earlier this month, Kerry was also charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Speaking on Thursday, Conservative shadow Commons leader Jesse Norman accused Burnham of breaching Parliament's sub judice rule, which says MPs should not refer to pending court cases in order to avoid influencing the outcome.

He added that the prime minister's comments at PMQs had "breached the legal presumption of innocence".

He asked Commons leader Sir Alan Campbell, a government minister, to "correct the record, withdraw the remark and apologise on behalf of the prime minister".

In response, Sir Alan said the prime minister had "said that he misspoke, he has apologised and he has corrected the record".

"There is no excuse for misspeaking in the House and I am not trying to explain that away, but this prime minister is characterised by an authenticity and a passion in the way that he responds," he added.

"It is not unusual for prime ministers or anybody else to misspeak in the House.

"As long as they correct the record, which he has done, that should be put into perspective."

stories.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay. As the petition explains: Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology. We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting. This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following SIREN v. San Jose. Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree. Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition Read the press release Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay

stories.summary: EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post. The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has published a summary of findings from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process. TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “ committed to protecting traveler privacy ,” the audit highlights that this has not been the case. The OIG found that TSA’s Credential Authentication Technology 2’s (CAT-2) vendor “was able to access and extract sensitive passenger information, including driver’s license and passport images, during system troubleshooting and enhancements, without TSA’s knowledge.” The OIG further admonished the agency: TSA lacked clear policies, did not track when this data was extracted, could not verify that extracted information was properly deleted, and did not notify passengers when their biometric and biographic information may have been stored. As a result, although passenger information was generally protected during routine operations, weaknesses in vendor oversight created a risk that sensitive personal information could be retained or exposed. We hope the TSA will fix these issues. In the original 1998 version of the game, he’d rip off players as they funnelled rupees and fudged the then still novel analogue-stick aiming. But in 2026 we have more responsive frame rates and a motion-controlled slingshot that allows precision adjustments. His targets tumble on the first go, and with them his entire business model. Even in Hyrule, the death of the high street seems inevitable. Bad news for him but great news for Link, a child of the forest who, as in 1998, steps into a vast fantasy kingdom to vanquish a great evil, but now does so with a number of improvements. The boy can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies to zip across grassy plains. He has a manual jump, free-rotating camera, a scrolling inventory bar that replaces menu screen faff and, crucially, a fatter wallet for holding all those gems he fleeces from struggling shooting gallery owners. stories.title: 'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
stories.summary: US inflation continues to rise, and this month the jump was above forecasts. Here's how some are surviving.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Kathryn Vaughn works many odd jobs to supplement her teacher's salary

Published 14 October 2026

Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years.

The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything".

She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise .

Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers for September that were released on Wednesday. The price rise was more than economists and Wall Street analysts had forecast.

High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans.

Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family.

"I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark."

Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money.

And it is still not enough to support her family.

Vaughn said she had to cancel a trip to see her parents because she couldn't afford gas

Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home.

"I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said.

The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult.

And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline.

"I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (£4.5)," he said.

Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control."

Punal Bhavsar says he can't afford a home with interest rates as high as they are

He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up.

The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, the index was -40. In May, it reached -45, the lowest since 2022.

A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis.

This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that.

When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef."

As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said.

Caitlin Green says she's had to get creative with recipes because of the high cost of beef

Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken.

"[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said.

Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month.

"I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically."

For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming.

She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies.

Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice.

The family has even decided to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much.

"It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot."

stories.title: Trump Says the Border Is Secure. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Keeps Declaring an Emergency.
stories.summary: The post Trump Says the Border Is Secure. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Keeps Declaring an Emergency. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A photo collage featuring a portrait of Texas Governor Greg Abbott surrounded by official state seal stamps, date stamps, border wall imagery, and clips of text declaring a state of disaster.
stories.body:
Since Texas Gov. Greg Abbott first declared an emergency at the border in 2021, he’s renewed or amended the proclamation at least 69 times. The proclamation has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state Legislature.

Co-published with The Texas Tribune

Last month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott repeated a claim he’s made for the past five years. He stated that the number of people crossing the Texas-Mexico border illegally “posed an ongoing and imminent threat” across the state. In doing so, he renewed a border security disaster proclamation that has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state Legislature.

Abbott’s declaration stands in sharp contrast to the numbers reported by the Trump administration, which says the drop in the flow of migrants crossing the border has been unprecedented and has reached historic lows since it took over in January 2025.

Yet, since Abbott first declared an emergency at the border during the Biden administration in 2021, he’s renewed or amended the proclamation at least 69 times — 21 of those during Trump’s tenure.

The Republican governor, who is running for his fourth term next month, has consolidated power like no Texas governor before him, building on his predecessors’ efforts to strengthen what by design is supposed to be a “weak governor” state as the constitution limits what can be done without legislative approval, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune have reported. One of the methods he’s used to do that is issuing executive orders and disaster declarations that allow him to shift funds, suspend regulations and award no-bid contracts at times of emergency.

Since January 2025, two of the top agencies involved with border enforcement — the Department of Public Safety and the Texas Military Department — have awarded more than $5 million in noncompetitive contracts citing the emergency for items like a Ford F-150, rifles and apartments, state records show.

“I think it’s unprecedented,” said Cal Jillson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas. “I don’t think that there is a similar example, certainly not as to the length of the emergency, and certainly not after the emergency has seemed to pass.”

Abbott’s office did not respond to specific questions for this story, including about the noncompetitive contracts, but Deputy Press Secretary Madeline Waschak said in a written statement that the governor has been clear that border security is an ongoing priority.

“The damage caused by four years of failed border policies under Democrat rule did not disappear overnight, and the progress we have made will not sustain itself without continued vigilance,” she wrote.

“Securing the border requires constant, deliberate action to combat illegal crossings, cartel smuggling, fentanyl trafficking, and other criminal activity that threatens public safety in Texas. Governor Abbott will ensure the tools remain in place to safeguard our state as we work alongside the Trump Administration to deter, arrest, detain, and deport illegal immigrants,” she added.

At the time of Abbott’s first border declaration, four months into President Joe Biden’s term, Border Patrol was making more than 180,000 apprehensions along the southwest border in a single month. According to Abbott, the federal government’s inability or unwillingness to enforce immigration laws had created a humanitarian crisis in many communities in Texas.

“The Biden Administration’s open-border policies have enabled escalating violence from the cartels, dramatically increased the risk of human trafficking, and created a severe crisis of illegal drugs crossing into the United States,” the order stated .

Since then, apprehensions along the southwest border have dropped on average to about 8,000 a month this year.

The border security declaration remains Abbott’s longest continuously running emergency proclamation. Abbott similarly renewed his 2020 COVID-19 disaster declaration for three years, even as he downplayed the severity of the pandemic.

“This is the quiet power of the governor,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston. “It’s not something often that they brag about because the more that it becomes a political issue, the more that there might be some contestation of it.”

Other than border security, the governor’s second longest-running emergency declaration is related to droughts. He declared a state disaster in July 2022 and within days amended it bringing the total of counties to 189. He’s continued to renew it, but now it applies to about a third of the counties originally identified.

State lawmakers have repeatedly tried — and failed — to curb the governor’s powers under the state’s disaster act. Last year, legislators from both parties filed at least a handful of measures that would mandate Abbott get approval from the Legislature if he wanted to extend a disaster declaration, but none passed.

Abbott’s emergency declarations have been accompanied by record spending on border security efforts. Texas budgeted over $11 billion during the Biden administration and allotted an additional $3 billion last year, after Trump took office.

It’s all part of Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, an initiative he launched in March 2021 contending it was needed to stem the smuggling of drugs and people into the country through Texas. Because of the emergency declaration, police could charge immigrants with criminal trespassing for crossing the border through private property, and the governor was able to shift money from other agencies to fund the operation and build border barriers, deploy the National Guard and get help from other states.

Much of the funding for Operation Lone Star is funneled through the Texas Military Department and DPS, two of the agencies responsible for major enforcement efforts. But the governor’s share of border spending has also ballooned since Abbott took office over a decade ago. State lawmakers allotted his office nearly $230 million last year to distribute through grants, largely to local prosecutors and government agencies helping the state with Operation Lone Star.

Though the situation on the ground has changed, one aspect of the emergency declaration has remained constant: the ability of state agencies to award noncompetitive contracts.

DPS and the Texas Military Department have awarded at least six noncompetitive contracts so far during the second Trump administration for work related to the operation where they cite an emergency. This includes a more than $2 million contract to Texas-based CTC Gunworks LLC for rifles and pistols for active-duty personnel. CTC Gunworks officials could not be reached for comment.

Officials with the Texas Military Department referred questions about its procurement process to the governor’s office. A DPS spokesperson said in a written statement that even though the disaster declaration allows for expedited purchases, the department still follows best practices and “aims to select vendors offering the best value, determined by cost, quality, and ability to meet the specific disaster response requirements.”

Regarding the specific contracts, the DPS spokesperson said they were purchases tied to existing state contracts.

The continued funding and expansion of Operation Lone Star has come even as it’s been plagued with problems. In 2022, an investigation by ProPublica, the Tribune and The Marshall Project found that the state’s reported success included arrests unrelated to the border or immigration and counted drug seizures made by troopers from across the state who were not directly assigned to the operation. The Tribune and Army Times also exposed poor working conditions, pay delays and suicides among National Guard members deployed as part of Operation Lone Star.

During a Tribune-hosted event this week with state lawmakers from El Paso, Democratic state Rep. Mary González , vice chair of the Appropriations Committee, said state legislators have already started to scale back when it comes to border funding and there’s interest from both sides of the aisle to continue to do so in the upcoming legislative session.

“I think that the problem is that some of that border security money still lies in the governor’s office which has no checks and balances and because we are still under an emergency — which is not an emergency anymore — an emergency border security statement which he can just use that money, you have seen some questionable appropriations under the veil of border security,” she said.

Abbott, however, has repeatedly said that Texas’ work in securing the border is not over.

“We must secure the border not just for the next two years of the Trump administration, but we gotta do it forever,” Abbott said at a press conference in early October where he discussed the federal government’s $7.5 billion reimbursement for border security expenses the state had incurred.

Rottinghaus said that Texas will always have to confront border crossings and drug trafficking, but the existence of those problems don’t always justify an emergency declaration.

“Even someone who strongly supports the governor’s board of policies might ask whether they want a future governor of the opposite party using the same interpretation of emergency authority for years,” Rottinghaus said, adding that the issue is that “governors, once they get a power, are hesitant to give it back.”

stories.body:
Years of antibiotic use have fuelled a rise in bacteria that can survive antibiotics. These antibiotic resistant bacteria are competing with and displacing other bacteria that are naturally present in the human gut, where they play a critical role in maintaining good health. Resistant bacteria have led to increased illness and death from diseases that were once easily treatable with antibiotics. Disease ecologist Eric Ng'eno shares findings from his research on how some resistant strains of Escherichia coli bacteria are taking over the guts of people who are otherwise healthy. He suggests how this displacement can be slowed down.

What did you do that’s new?

In every person’s gut there are millions of friendly microbes that help digest food, produce energy, and shield the person from harmful, disease-causing bacteria and other invaders. The microbes that live in the body include bacteria, fungi and viruses. They form a community of microorganisms.

Where people live and work together, healthy microbes spread easily through everyday interactions like handshakes, kissing, and sharing food or water. In this way, people who interact often tend to develop similar gut microbes. We call these the background microbial community.

Disease-causing agents spread in a similar way.

Microorganisms affect the environment around them so as to encourage or prevent the growth of other microorganisms in their community. We wanted to assess whether these microbial interactions play a role in the presence of resistant E. coli in the gut of individuals living in a densely populated urban informal settlement in Nairobi, Kenya.

To do this, we mapped out background microbial communities in people living in different areas across the study region.

We then tested how different background microbial composition identified at the beginning of the study were associated with resistance patterns observed thereafter.

How did you go about it?

To determine the role of the gut microbes, we first built a statistical model that used all three factors that contribute to the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria together. These factors are:

antibiotic use

spread of bacteria

background microbial communities in people’s guts.

We measured how well this combined model predicted where resistant E. coli appeared.

Next, we ran a similar model, but this time using background microbial communities as the only predictor. These are the microbes people naturally had in their gut at the beginning of the study.

By comparing the two results, we were able to pinpoint how much the background microbial communities alone drove resistance in this setting. We used E. coli strains identified from faecal samples collected from people living in different locations across the whole study area.

The idea of considering microbial interactions in the analysis of drivers of resistant bacteria carriage isn’t new. But this is the first time where such interactions were considered in an analysis of real-world data.

What did you find?

We showed that the background microbial community largely determined which E.coli strains people in this area ended up carrying.

People who lived in areas where invading resistant bacteria made up a larger share of the local microbial community were more likely to carry resistant E. coli strains. Those in areas where the local microbial communities mostly included the native non-resistant bacteria were less likely to carry resistant E.coli strains. This was the case despite how antibiotics were used and how easily bacteria could spread in these areas.

Antibiotic use and background microbial communities work together. When antibiotics disrupted the gut microbiota of individuals, the native microbes that people had in their guts were quickly displaced by microbial communities present in the surrounding environment. If these replacement microbial communities include invading resistant bacteria, they may create an environment that supports growth of even more resistant bacteria in the invaded guts.

How this process worked varied with the type of antibiotics involved.

Antibiotics that severely disrupted the gut microbiota facilitated direct takeover by microbes present in the surrounding environment.

On the other hand, milder, less universally lethal antibiotics tended to result in varied outcomes. The resistant E. coli has fewer opportunities to take over since these antibiotics preserve the original gut microbiota that compete with incoming microbes.

Why are your findings useful?

These findings highlight that carriage of antibiotic resistant E. coli in community settings is context dependent. Native microbes present in the broader environment shape whether an invading resistant strain established itself or not.

Strategies to minimise antibiotic resistance need, therefore, to be tailored to the local microbial community context. In areas where the background microbial community includes resistant types, measures which minimise disruption or facilitate the spread of harmless microbes should be encouraged.

Broadly speaking, current preventive efforts should always aim at helping natural, diverse, non-resistant microbial communities to reclaim their ground in human populations.

These communities carry the potential for holding back resistant bacteria. The goal is to preserve them.

Minimising the use of antibiotics is key to this effort. Vaccines and hygiene practices which minimise the risk for diseases can help reduce the need for antibiotics.

Where unavoidable, antibiotics need to be used carefully. In addition, there need to be efforts to restore microbes lost with antibiotic use.

In the short term, using probiotics after using antibiotics may be a good strategy. For the long term, people could be encouraged to embrace “farming of the microbiome”. This describes the continuous efforts of creating a culture of good bacteria in the body. People around the world have been doing this for centuries through eating fermented foods, for example, which are naturally packed with the good microbes.

stories.body:
Ethiopia has experienced recurrent conflicts for over five decades. This includes a long-running civil war sparked by the overthrow of Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974, renewed fighting in Tigray, and ongoing conflicts in Amhara and Oromia .

The renewed hostilities in Tigray threaten to undo a peace process that had begun with an agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in 2022.

Why has peace been so difficult to sustain in Ethiopia? My research on constitutional design and conflict points to four interconnected explanations:

the foundations of the Ethiopian state remain contested

ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements

armed force continues to be a route to political power

regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts.

The problem isn’t that Ethiopians of diverse ethnic backgrounds hate one another and can’t live together peacefully. It’s that successive political arrangements have failed to establish widely accepted rules for managing disagreements.

1. The foundations of the state remain contested

Ethiopia’s 1995 constitution emerged from a political transition that followed the overthrow of the military government in 1991. This ended nearly two decades of civil war .

The new leadership sought to address long-standing grievances over ethnic marginalisation and demands for greater autonomy. It restructured the country as a federation largely organised around ethnolinguistic communities. The constitution vested sovereignty in Ethiopia’s nations, nationalities and peoples. It guaranteed their right to self-determination, including secession .

Proponents of federalism regard this right as protection against historical domination. Opponents argue that it entrenches ethnic boundaries and encourages competition over territory and resources .

Ethnic diversity doesn’t inevitably lead to violence. And federalism isn’t inherently destabilising. It was introduced to accommodate competing national claims within a common political order.

But constitutional recognition is not the same as political reconciliation.

Read more: What is federalism? Why Ethiopia uses this system of government and why it’s not perfect

The problem arises when a constitution sets out rules for sharing power and governing the country without sufficient agreement among the political groups expected to follow them. Instead of providing a common framework for resolving disputes, those rules become another source of political conflict .

2. Ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements

The 2022 Pretoria agreement was about stopping hostilities, not about resolving their causes. The federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front agreed to end two years of war. Major political questions were left for later negotiation.

Disputed territories, regional administration, political participation and accountability for wartime abuses remain contentious .

Eritrea, a major participant in the 2020-2022 war in Tigray, did not sign the agreement. Eritrean forces are still present in parts of Tigray.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front itself also became fragmented after the war. Divisions emerged within the leadership. Disagreements over federal relations, political authority and control of military forces developed into a struggle within the movement.

A peace agreement assumes that the parties signing it have authority over their political and military organisations to honour their commitments. But when these organisations fragment, it becomes unclear who can carry out agreements.

The Tigray leadership’s loss of legal party status in 2025 added another obstacle to political reintegration.

These developments have undermined confidence that the transition from armed conflict to constitutional politics would be honoured.

Read more: Ethiopia’s peace deal is unravelling – what went wrong with the Tigray agreement

This distinction is fundamental. A cessation of hostilities can save lives immediately. But it cannot, by itself, establish a legitimate regional government, resolve territorial claims or restore trust between former enemies.

3. Armed force is a route to political power

The use of violence to acquire or retain political authority has deep roots in Ethiopia’s modern history. In 1974 , the military overthrew the empire-state and established a military regime. This regime was itself overthrown in 1991 by a coalition of rebel forces led by the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front.

These transitions reinforced a pattern in which political power could be won through armed struggle. When political opponents have little confidence that elections, courts or negotiations can bring change, taking up arms can appear more effective than peaceful political competition.

The continued use of force by both the state and armed groups makes this cycle difficult to break .

Read more: Ethiopia’s national dialogue was meant to heal the nation, but divisions are deepening

Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018 after years of anti-government protests and divisions within the ruling coalition. Two years later, rising political tensions led to war in Tigray. Abiy’s regime has faced accusations of serious rights abuses and a lack of accountability.

This has deepened distrust. It’s made negotiated settlements harder to achieve. Under Abiy, political authority has become increasingly personalised. Military operations and extraordinary security measures have been used to confront political challenges.

Peace needs a political environment where losing an election doesn’t mean exclusion from power or exposure to coercion.

4. Regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts

Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts are increasingly intersecting with the interests and actions of neighbouring countries. Eritrean forces fought beside Ethiopia’s army in Tigray. They remained in parts of the region after the 2022 peace deal. Now the former allies are adversaries .

There have been accusations of cross-border military intervention . This has renewed concerns that the war in Tigray could develop into a wider conflict.

Ethiopia’s ambitions to secure Red Sea access have further complicated relations with Eritrea and Somalia. Its 2024 agreement with Somaliland provoked a dispute with Mogadishu.

Ethiopia also has strained relations with Egypt over its mega dam in the Nile River . Sudan’s ongoing civil war and rival Saudi Arabia and Emirati relationships across the Red Sea add further pressures .

Read more: Ethiopia and Eritrea are on edge again: what’s behind the growing risk of war

These external tensions can make domestic troubles harder to contain. Ethiopia has a duty to defend its boundaries and also to respect those of its neighbours.

What would lasting peace require?

These four obstacles to peace reinforce one another:

disagreements over constitutional rules fuel political tensions

armed conflict makes inclusive negotiations more difficult

peace agreements that fail to address underlying grievances leave the door open to renewed violence

competing regional interests complicate efforts to achieve lasting peace.

As a result, Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts cannot be resolved through ceasefires alone.

Lasting peace requires all Ethiopians to agree on how power is shared, and the relationship between the federal government and its regions.

Read more: What makes peace talks successful? The 4 factors that matter

But resolving Ethiopia’s internal divisions will not, on its own, settle tensions with neighbouring countries. That requires diplomacy built on respect for sovereignty, non-interference and peaceful negotiation over interests.

Ethiopia therefore faces two interconnected challenges. First, building a political system that its diverse communities can accept. Second, establishing peaceful relations with its neighbours.

Lasting peace depends on both.
